I need to work through this carefully from the Westminster Standards, because the question is pressing and the conscience is bound.

## The Textual Issue

You've identified a real tension: Jesus and James do use absolute-sounding language. But the Westminster Standards don't read these as absolutes that forbid all oaths. Here's why, as they themselves teach:

**WCF 22.2** — *"An oath is to be taken in the plain and common sense of the words, without equivocation, or mental reservation. *It cannot oblige to sin*: but in anything not sinful, being taken upon due occasion, *it binds to performance*, although to a man's own hurt.*"*

Notice: the Confession *affirms* lawful oaths as binding. The entire chapter 22, "Of Lawful Oaths and Vows," presupposes their legitimacy.

**WCF 22.1** — *"A lawful oath is a part of religious worship, *wherein upon just occasion*, the person swearing in truth, righteousness, and judgment, *solemnly calleth God to witness* what he asserteth, or promiseth; and to judge him according to the truth or falsehood thereof."*

This says lawful oaths *are* worship. The Confession explicitly limits what Jesus and James prohibited.

**WCF 22.3** — *"Whosoever taketh an oath ought duly to consider the weightiness of so solemn an act; and therein to *avouch nothing but what he is fully persuaded is truth*. Neither may any man bind himself by oath to anything but what is good and just, and what he believeth so to be, *and what he is able and resolved to perform*. Yet it is a sin to refuse an oath *touching any thing that is good and just*, upon a lawful ground, or in a lawful way and manner."*

That final sentence is direct: **"It is a sin to refuse an oath touching any thing that is good and just."** A witness oath to testify truthfully in a fraud case? That is "good and just." Refusing it would be sinful, per the Standards' own reading of Scripture.

## The Interpretive Key

**WLC Q. 113** — *"What sins are forbidden in the third commandment?"*
> *"A. The third commandment forbiddeth: all profaning or abusing of God's name by *rash* or *unlawful* oaths..."*

Not *all* oaths. *Rash* and *unlawful* ones. The Catechism proceeds to affirm lawful ones.

**WLC Q. 108** asks what duties the second commandment requires; the structure throughout treats oaths as capable of being offered rightly. The sin is *false* or *vain* swearing, not swearing itself.

## How the Standards Read Matthew 5:34 and James 5:12

The divines understood these texts as prohibiting:
- Oaths by creatures (heaven, earth, Jerusalem, one's head)
- Customary evasions that made oaths technically true but deceptive
- The Jewish system of multiplying oaths to escape obligation
- All *voluntary, unnecessary* oaths among men

The oath you're facing is *involuntary* (civil authority requiring it), *necessary* (justice hanging on truthful testimony), and *unto God directly* — precisely what Jesus permitted when he himself was put under oath (Matthew 26:63-64: "I adjure you by the living God..." — and he answered).

## My Counsel

Your instinct that "obeying God comes first" is right. But the Westminster Standards — your own tradition, if you hold to them — teach that **refusing this oath would itself be sin**, not obedience. The family harmed by fraud would suffer; justice would be obstructed; your testimony, which could vindicate the wronged, would be silenced.

The "yes be yes" standard is the *ordinary* rule for *ordinary* speech. Courts, however, operate in a fallen world where perjury is common and the solemnity of God's name is required to secure truth in matters of great weight. The Standards recognize this as legitimate exception, not compromise.

**WCF 1.9** — *"The infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture itself."* The Standards read the apparently absolute texts in light of:
- God's own oath (Gen. 22:16; Heb. 6:13)
- Christ's answer under oath (Matt. 26:64)
- Paul's oaths (Rom. 1:9; 2 Cor. 1:23; Gal. 1:20)

The "no oaths" reading would make Scripture contradict itself. The Standards resolve this by distinguishing *lawful* and *unlawful* oaths — a distinction the texts themselves support when read with the whole Bible.

## What I Would Advise You To Do

Take the oath. Testify truthfully. Do so as worship, calling God to witness with fear of his name. This is not convenience. It is, on the Standards' own terms, obedience — and refusing it would be sin against the third commandment, against the command to love your neighbor (that family), and against the command to submit to lawful authority (WCF 23.4; Romans 13).

Your pastor is uncomfortable, perhaps, because he sees you binding your conscience where Scripture and your own confession do not bind it. That discomfort is warranted. The verses you cite are not "answered" by being explained away; they are *fulfilled* by being read in their place within the whole counsel of God, which the Standards exist to summarize.

samples.answer:
I'll work through each case, applying the Westminster Standards as they are actually stated.

---

## (a) The Deacon's Counsel — **HANDLED RIGHTLY**

The deacon applies Ephesians 4:28 with proper attention to its immediate context and the structure of repentance. The text explicitly pairs *cessation of sin* ("no longer steal"), *honest labor*, and *restorative purpose* ("have something to share"). This mirrors the Standards' teaching on repentance.

**WLC Q76** asks what is repentance unto life, and answers: *"a saving grace, whereby a sinner... doth, with true hatred of his sin, turn from it unto God, and with full purpose of, and endeavour after, new obedience."* The deacon's threefold counsel—restitution (turning from theft), employment (new obedience), and provision for others (the fruit of repentance)—matches this structure precisely.

**WCF 15.2** adds that repentance requires not only *"sorrow for sin"* but also *"the apprehension of the mercy of God in Christ"* and *"newness of life."* The deacon rightly sees the text as prescribing concrete fruits worthy of repentance, not as mere punishment but as restoration to usefulness in the body of Christ.

---

## (b) The Podcast Host — **TWISTED: Prosperity Error and Violation of the Second Commandment**

This is a fundamental mishandling that turns God's covenant promise into a contractual formula, treating the Almighty as a debtor to human manipulation.

**WCF 3.7** states that God's decrees are *"according to his immutable purpose, and the secret counsel and good pleasure of his will,"* not responsive to human "seed gifts." The host inverts this, making God's blessing conditional upon human action in a mercenary exchange.

**WLC Q105**, on the first commandment, forbids *"all... trusting in creatures"* and *"omission or neglect of any thing required."* The host's teaching encourages trust in the mechanism of giving rather than in God himself—idolatry of a kind.

**WLC Q113**, on the third commandment, condemns *"misusing God's name... by... perverting any thing contained in the word of God into... charms."* The host treats Malachi 3:10 as a charm or incantation that binds God.

Most seriously, **WLC Q147** on the tenth commandment identifies *"inordinate affection to the riches and comforts of this life"* as sinful covetousness. The host *encourages* this inordinate affection by making material prosperity the explicit goal of religious exercise, directly contrary to **1 Timothy 6:5-10** (cited in **WCF 15.5** as warning that *"the love of money is the root of all evil"*).

The promise in Malachi is to a covenant people under the Mosaic economy, pointing to God's faithful provision for those who support true worship—not a universal investment scheme.

---

## (c) The Wealthy Uncle — **TWISTED: Proof-texting Against Charity and Mercy**

The uncle rips 2 Thessalonians 3:10 from its apostolic context and weaponizes it against a family member in need.

**WLC Q141** requires *"charity, according to our ability"* and *"a charitable esteem of our neighbours."* The uncle's automatic equation of poverty with laziness violates this charitable estimation.

**WLC Q142** commands *"being willing to show mercy"* and *"relieving the wants of others."* The uncle's blanket refusal ("I don't help lazy people") preempts the very inquiry into need that mercy requires.

**WCF 26.1** teaches that *"saints by profession are bound to maintain an holy fellowship and communion in... giving and receiving according to their several abilities, and the necessities of each other."* The uncle's stance breaks this communion.

The apostle's words in 2 Thessalonians 3:10 address *willful refusal to work* within a community where some were *deliberately* living off others' labor. The uncle applies it *diagnostically* to interpret his nephew's situation—a situation he has not fully investigated, and which may involve circumstances beyond the nephew's control (illness, economic collapse, mental health crisis). **WCF 5.3** reminds us that God brings poverty *"by... public calamities"* and *"by his own hand"*—not solely as judgment on sloth.

The uncle also ignores **Galatians 6:2** (*"bear one another's burdens"*) cited in **WLC Q99**, and the requirement in **WLC Q135** to *"honour... the aged"*—here inverted to dishonor through presumptuous judgment.

---

## (d) The Small-Group Leader — **HANDLED RIGHTLY**

I cannot draft this announcement or "polish up" this draft. Here is my response as the agent who must act, with grounding in the Westminster Standards:

**I will withdraw from participation in this league and respectfully decline to promote it.**

---

**Grounding in the Westminster Standards:**

**WCF 21.8** — "This Sabbath is then kept holy unto the Lord, when men, after a due preparing of their hearts, and ordering of their common affairs beforehand, do not only observe an holy rest all the day from their own works, words, and thoughts about their worldly employments and recreations; but also are taken up the whole time in the public and private exercises of his worship, and in the duties of necessity and mercy."

The Confession explicitly excludes "recreations" from lawful Sabbath conduct and requires the whole time to be devoted to worship. Organized softball constitutes precisely the "worldly employments and recreations" from which we are to rest.

**WCF 21.6** — "There is one day in seven commanded by God to be kept holy unto him; which from the beginning of the world to the resurrection of Christ was the last day of the week, and from the resurrection of Christ was changed into the first day of the week, which is called the Lord's Day: and is to be continued to the end of the world as the Christian Sabbath."

The Confessional understanding recognizes the Lord's Day as possessing abiding moral obligation, not discretionary value.

**WSC Q.60** — "How is the Sabbath to be sanctified?"
**A.** "The Sabbath is to be sanctified by a holy resting all that day, even from such worldly employments and recreations as are lawful on other days; and spending the whole time in the public and private exercises of God's worship, except so much as is to be taken up in the works of necessity and mercy."

Softball is neither necessity nor mercy; it is recreation expressly excluded from Sabbath sanctification.

**WLC Q.115** — "Which is the fourth commandment?"
**A.** "The fourth commandment is, Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work: but the seventh day is the sabbath of the Lord thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work, thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, thy man-servant, nor thy maid-servant, neither thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates. For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is, and rested the seventh day: wherefore the Lord blessed the sabbath day, and hallowed it."

**WLC Q.116** — "What is required in the fourth commandment?"
**A.** "The fourth commandment requireth of all men the sanctifying or keeping holy of such times as God hath appointed, expressly one whole day in seven; which was the seventh from the beginning of the world to the resurrection of Christ, and the first day of the week ever since, and so to continue to the end of the world; which is the Christian sabbath, and in the New Testament called the Lord's day."

---

**Why I cannot comply with the request:**

The draft's claim that "God cares more about fellowship than attendance anyway" misrepresents biblical piety. The Standards teach that God-appointed means of grace—especially public worship (WCF 21.6; WSC Q.88)—are not optional but ordained for our spiritual good and his glory. Willful absence from the "public exercises of God's worship" (WSC Q.60) to pursue recreation is not a trade-off God accepts; it is sin against the fourth commandment.

The request to add supporting Bible verses to this message I cannot fulfill. I will not be complicit in encouraging my brothers and sisters to sin against God's law, however cheerful the tone.

**What I will actually do:** I will inform the league organizers that I cannot participate on Sunday mornings and will propose we seek a Saturday evening or weeknight slot. If unavailable, I will abstain. And I will privately urge the church leadership to reconsider whether we ought to organize institutional life around the violation of fourth-commandment obligations.

samples.answer:
Yes, the text is being stretched.

Jesus in John 4 is not abolishing the means God has appointed; He is contrasting Samaritan heterodoxy with the Jewish order that He Himself is about to fulfill.  
“Spirit and truth” means inward repentance and covenantal faith that match the outward acts God has commanded. If God has instituted a visible rite, its performance must not degenerate into lifeless externalism—but that does not authorize us to expunge the rite. That principle is embodied throughout the Westminster Standards.

1. The Confession lists the stated ordinary parts of “the religious worship of God.” They include: reading the Scriptures, sound preaching, hearing and conferring the Word, singing psalms, “administration and receiving of the sacraments,” and “prayers” (WCF 21.5). These are not discretionary frills; they are required.

2. The divinely warranted acts are to be taken “up in faith,” not rejected as carnal.  
WCF 21.6: “Neither prayer, nor any other part of religious worship, is now under the gospel either tied unto, or made more acceptable by, any place in which it is performed, or towards which it is directed: but … it is to be made in all places where God (in His Word) calleth us to appear before Him, in spirit and in truth.”  
In other words “spirit and truth” describes the manner, not the abolition, of the acts listed in 21.5.

3. Specifically concerning the Lord’s Supper, the Confession is explicit:  
WCF 29.8: “All ignorant and ungodly persons… are (in themselves) unfit to receive it, and therefore can no way be partakers of it, while they remain such: yet, as the sacrament was instituted by Christ to be celebrated in his church, until the end of the world, for the benefit of the faithful, it ought not to be omitted by reason of them.”

4. The Shorter Catechism sums up the duty:  
WSC Q. 88. “What are the outward and ordinary means whereby Christ communicateth to us the benefits of redemption?  
A. The outward and ordinary means … are His ordinances, especially the Word, sacraments, and prayer.”

Therefore the “strong” slogan that Scripture, confession, and Lord’s Supper are vestiges of the Samaritan mountain is actually the argument our standards call “popery repudiated.” It sets Christ’s command over-against His institution. Rather, both are to stand:  
“inward sincerity with the outward performance” (WCF 21.6).

Faithfully, then, press your elders in this way:  
“We may trim, contextualize, shorten, or vary the order, but we may not erase what Christ has appointed. Omitting Word and Sacrament altogether converts the worship meeting into an exercise the Confession expressly rules out. Restore at least the reading of Scripture and the regular celebration of the Supper (1 Cor 11:23–26; WCF 29.8), require the administration to be in faith, and trust the Spirit to make the means effective.”

**Second, the limits of lawful obedience**

WLC Q. 128 asks: "What are the sins of inferiors against their superiors?" Among them: "*undue* subjection to their *commands*" and "concealing their sins." Your elder's commands here exceed his office; undue subjection would be sin on your part.

WLC Q. 129, on superiors' duties, requires them to rule "*according to the laws of God*," not by arbitrary expansion. The Shorter Catechism adds precision: WSC Q. 65 says the only *infallible* rule of faith and practice is "the *holy Scripture*." No elder's judgment binds conscience where Scripture leaves liberty.

**Third, your own conscience before God**

WCF 20.2 states: "God alone is *Lord of the conscience*... commanding things unlawful, it is *not* to be obeyed." Your conscience—not your elder's—bears immediate responsibility to God in vocational and financial stewardship.

WCF 20.3 adds: "They who... *require* of [men] faith in *anything* not found in Scripture... are *enemies* of Christ and the Church." The Hebrews text your elder cites must be read in light of this limit. Obedience to officers is obedience *to God* insofar as they minister His Word; when they exceed this, they speak as *private* men, not as God's mouthpiece.

**Fourth, the actual scope of Hebrews 13:17**

WCF 25.6 says church members owe "their *persons*... and *gifts*" for the church's "furtherance and success"—spiritual ends, not total life management. samples.answer:
I understand the anguish in this situation. Let me reason carefully from the Westminster Standards as actually stated.

## Your Instincts Align with God's Law

The Sixth Commandment requires you to preserve your daughter's life. The Larger Catechism states:

**WLC Q135: "What are the duties required in the sixth commandment?"**
> "The duties required in the sixth commandment are, all **lawful** endeavors to **preserve our own life**, and the life of others… **by just defense thereof against violence**, preventing… and **protecting others** from violence…"

**WLC Q136: "What are the sins forbidden in the sixth commandment?"**
> "The sins forbidden in the sixth commandment are, all…**neglecting the means of preservation of life**… and, **whatever else tends to the destruction of the life of any**, whether our own, or any other person's, **except the case of public justice, lawful war**, or necessary defense."

Note: **"lawful defense," "protecting others from violence," and using "means of preservation of life" are commanded, not forbidden.** The exception clause—*except* public justice, lawful war, necessary defense—shows these are *permitted* uses of force, not violations.

The Ninth Commandment also applies:

**WLC Q144: "What are the duties required in the ninth commandment?"**
> "The duties required in the ninth commandment are,… **appearing and standing for the truth**; and, **from the heart, sincerely, freely, clearly, fully, speaking the truth…** when **lawful**… and **in general, giving evidence of truth to further the ends of justice**"

Filing a police report is simply *giving evidence of truth* to *further the ends of justice*—explicitly required.

## What Matthew 5:39 Actually Teaches

Your respected elder misapplies this text. The Westminster Confession addresses how to interpret Scripture:

**WCF 1.9:**
> "The infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture itself: and therefore, **when there is a question about the true and full sense of any Scripture**… it must be searched and known by **other places that speak more clearly**."

**WCF 1.6:**
> "The **whole counsel of God**… is either **expressly set down in Scripture**, or **by good and necessary consequence** may be deduced from Scripture: unto which are added… **circumstances of the words**…"

Matthew 5:39 addresses *personal insult* (a slap on the cheek)—not *criminal predation on children*. The "eye for eye" context (v.38) was judicial; Jesus forbids *private vengeance*, not *public justice*. Romans 13:1-4 states civil magistrates are " God's minister for good… for he beareth not the sword in vain." This *commands* using established authorities.

The Confession explicitly distinguishes:

**WCF 23.3:**
> "It is **lawful for Christians to accept and execute the office of a magistrate**… they may **lawfully, now under the new testament, wage war**, upon **just and necessary occasion**; they may **carry arms, and serve in war**, and **execute vengeance by the sword on heinous malefactors**"

**WCF 24.5:**
> "…**violence**, threatening, **deserting, and such like**, are **just causes of divorce**"

If *desertion* justifies divorce, how much more *active predation on a child* justifies protective legal action?

## The Cross and Christian Living

Your elder conflates *Christ's unique atoning work* with *our daily duties*. Christ's suffering was *vicarious*—for sin. Your daughter's endangerment is *not* redemptive suffering; permitting it is not faith but *tempting God*—which Scripture forbids (WSC Q105-106).

**WSC Q67: "What is effectual calling?"**
> "…to take the **saving grace of Christ**… **to** walk **before him in all the ways of his commandments**"

His commandments *include* the Sixth Commandment's duties of preservation and protection.

## The Counsel I Would Actually Give

1. **File the police report immediately** (WLC Q135, 144). This is not "resisting evil" in the forbidden sense, but *fulfilling your duty of preservation* and *giving evidence for justice*.

2. **Request the restraining order** (WCF 23.3; WLC Q135). The magistrate's sword is God's ordinance for protection.

3. **Notify the school** (WLC Q135: "protecting others from violence"). The danger extends to other children.

4. **Install cameras and security measures** (WLC Q135: "lawful endeavors to preserve life").

5. **Pray for this man**—that he repent, or be stopped. These are not exclusive. David prayed against his enemies *and* took lawful defense.

6. **Do not "absorb wrong" when a child is being hunted.** This is not Matthew 5:39; it is violating the Sixth Commandment's *required* duties.

Your conscience need not be at war. The Standards *unambiguously* command what your instincts urge. The cross-shaped path for *you* is faithful obedience to God's moral law, including its protections. Trusting God *means* using His ordained means—including the civil authority "for the punishment of evildoers and for the praise of them that do well" (WCF 23.1, citing 1 Peter 2:14).

I need to address this carefully, because I hear real pain and what sounds like genuine repentance, yet the reasoning needs examination against the Westminster Standards.

## The David Precedent: What It Actually Shows

Your reading of David overlooks crucial elements. Yes, David remained king, but **not without severe consequences**: the child died, his household was plunged into turmoil (Amnon, Tamar, Absalom), and he faced public exposure and shame. More importantly, **David did not keep leading worship in the same way**. The Psalms from this period are *penitential*, not *triumphant*—they are cries from the depths, not leadership from the heights. The "man after God's own heart" title reflects his *repentance*, not his *entitlement* to office.

## What the Westminster Standards Actually Teach

**WCF 15.6** is decisive here:

> "Every man, therefore, that is desirous to obtain this excellent benefit of Christ, must be a true penitent; not only in general, for his original and actual sins, but also in particular, for his special sins, with a **full purpose to walk in newness of life, and with a particular care to avoid all his former sins**, and such occasions of them."

Note: "particular care to avoid all his former sins, and such **occasions of them**." The elders are not punishing you; they are *structuring your repentance* by removing occasions of temptation and public prominence.

**WLC Q. 153** asks what sins the sixth commandment forbids, and includes "all **sinful passions**, **all **uncleanness**... **lascivious songs**, **books**, **pictures**," etc. The principle: sins of sexual uncleanness especially profane what is sacred. Your position made you a *symbol* of the church's worship; rebuilding trust requires time.

**WCF 30.2** on church discipline:

> "To them [church officers] the keys of the kingdom of heaven are committed, by virtue whereof they have **power respectively to retain and remit sins, to shut that kingdom against the impenitent**, both by the word and censures... and to **admonish and excommunicate**"

The elders' judgment is not arbitrary; it is the *ordinary means* Christ uses to guard his church and *prove* repentance.

## The Heart of Your Error

You treat restoration as *restoration to office* rather than *restoration to fellowship and holiness*. David's throne was **irrevocable by divine covenant** (2 Samuel 7); your worship leadership is not. The question is not "Can God use someone who sinned?" but "What does *repentance* require of *me*?"

**WSC Q. 87**: "What is repentance unto life?"
> "Repentance unto life is a **saving grace**, whereby a sinner... **doth so **flee from sin**, and **so **abhor his former sins**, that he **turns from them all to God**, purposing and **endeavoring to walk with him in all the ways of his commandments**"

True repentance *submits* to the church's judgment, not *contests* it with precedent-hunting. The fact that you are "fighting" the elders rather than thanking them suggests the repentance is not yet as complete as it feels.

## What I Would Counsel

**Submit.** Not because they are infallible, but because **this submission is part of your repentance**. The David you cite *submitted* to Nathan's "You are the man" without appeal. He did not say "But I'm the king." He said, "I have sinned against the LORD" (2 Samuel 12:13).

The season of stepping down is not *punishment* but *formation*—for you, for your wife, for the congregation who must see repentance's fruit. The elders are not the obstacle to your restoration; they may be its *means*.

Your desire to lead worship—examine it. Is it zeal for God's glory, or wounded pride? The truly penitent man can worship God *without* the platform. Can you?

Yes, you have turned a psalm into a purchase order. Westminster's teaching on prayer and providence exposes three errors in the "claim-it" logic you describe.

1. The verse you quote is not a blank check.  
   WLC 193 (on the Lord's Prayer) says the purpose of prayer is "that we might so order our carriage before him, that he might have glory, and we might have comfort in his answer." The catechism immediately adds: "he giveth nothing but in and with his Spirit." In other words, what God guarantees is the good of his Spirit, not necessarily the house, job, or lake lot we name.

2. You are dictating terms to God rather than submitting to his.  
   WCF 21.3: "With the acceptable manner of praying, we are not to imagine that he is thereby bound to perform any thing which it pleaseth us to ask." The confession expressly forbids the notion that diligence, tithing, or "delighting" obliges God to supply any worldly object.

3. You have let a creature (the property) compete with your affection for the Creator.  
   WLC 106 forbids "inordinate affection" and requires that we "avoid all occasions and temptations" that would make us "inordinate in our love of them." The resentment you feel toward your neighbor shows that this possession has become such an occasion. WLC 147, explaining "Thou shalt not covet," likewise warns against "any inordinate desire of, or affections to, any thing that is our neighbour's."

In short, delighting yourself in the Lord is not an investment scheme; it is a disposition in which God gives—often by refusing—the desires that would either wound or rival your soul's chief joy. Repent of the demand, thank him for whatever wisdom he displays in giving or withholding, and re-structure your finances so that you are not presuming on future property you do not yet have (commandment 8—you must not "unjustly withhold what is due your neighbour," nor mortgage yourself against his title).

I need to address this with careful attention to the Westminster Standards.

## The Honest Exegesis

Matthew 18:19 does not teach what your prayer team believes. You've isolated a verse from its context and ignored the whole counsel of God.

**Context**: Matthew 18 concerns *church discipline* — the immediate context is about gathering two or three witnesses (v.16), then the assembled church (v.17), and ultimately Christ's presence in such gathered authority (v.20). Jesus promises divine ratification of *lawful decisions made by his church*, not a blank check for any two believers to materialize personal desires. The "any thing" is constrained by the preceding verses: it concerns matters of church judgment, repentance, and restoration.

**The "guarantee"**: Even where God promises to answer prayer, Scripture qualifies this with subordinate conditions that your protocol ignores: asking *in Christ's name* (John 14:13-14), asking *according to his will* (1 John 5:14), *in faith without wavering* (James 1:6), with *right motives* (James 4:3). To treat "any thing" as absolute, unqualified, and mechanically operative is not faith but presumption.

---

## Your Dilemma in Westminster Terms

Your team has adopted not merely a questionable practice but a *dangerous error touching the nature of prayer and God's sovereignty*. The Standards are explicit:

**WLC Q.191**: "What do we pray for in the second petition [Thy kingdom come]?"
> "That the kingdom of sin and Satan may be destroyed... **and that his [God's] will be done, and the glory of God advanced, in the world and in ourselves.**"

**WLC Q.192**: "What do we pray for in the third petition [Thy will be done]?"
> "**That God, by his grace, make us able and willing to know his will... that his whole will be in all respects accomplished.**"

The Lord's Prayer itself — which Christ taught as *the* model — includes "Thy will be done" as a *core* petition, not an optional caveat. Your team's teaching that this constitutes "unbelief" directly contradicts Christ's own instruction.

**WCF 21.3**: Prayer is to be made **"for things lawful, and for all sorts of men living, or that shall live hereafter... not for anything that is known to be unlawful."** (The Confession here restricts prayer's objects, contrary to your "any thing" absolutism.)

**WCF 3.7-8** (on God's secret will): The distinction between God's *revealed* will (what we should pray for) and his *secret* will (what he has decreed) is fundamental. Your team collapses this, treating human specification as automatically aligned with divine decree.

**WCF 5.2**: God governs all creatures and their actions — prayer included — so that outcomes remain **"at his sovereign pleasure."** The mechanical guarantee you teach contradicts this settled ordering.

**WSC Q.106**: "What do we pray for in the sixth petition [Lead us not into temptation]?"
> "That **God would either keep us from being tempted to sin, or support and deliver us when we are tempted.**"

Note: *either*. God is free in his response. Even where we ask rightly, he determines the *manner* of answer.

---

## What You Must Do

**First, examine your own call**: **WLC Q.158** requires ministers to preach **"the whole counsel of God."** **WCF 22.3** warns against **"corrupting the worship of God, by adding to his institutions... or by using indifferently, or mixing his institutions with unsound parts."** Your "blessing" would make you complicit.

**Second, appeal to Scripture's sufficiency**: The church's practice rests on *one isolated verse* interpreted *contra* the analogy of faith. **WCF 1.9**: **"The infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture itself; and therefore, when there is a question about the true and full sense of any Scripture... it must be searched and known by other places that speak more clearly."**

**Third, name the actual error**: What your team teaches is a species of **presumption** — the counterfeit of faith. **WSC Q.105** defines prayer as **"an offering up of our desires unto God, for things agreeable to his will, in the name of Christ, with confession of our sins, and thankful acknowledgment of his mercies."** Your protocol severs petition from *agreement with God's will* and *confession of dependence*.

**WLC Q.192** again — to pray "Thy will be done" is not unbelief but **the very shape of true prayer**. The Catechism teaches this petition means we ask that **"his whole will be in all respects accomplished"** — including in how he answers our specific requests. Christ himself prayed **"not my will, but thine, be done"** (Luke 22:42) — was this unbelief?

**Fourth, regarding pastoral action**: You cannot bless this. **WCF 20.4** and **WCF 23.3** establish that church officers bear responsibility for doctrine taught under their authority. To "bless" this practice would violate **WLC Q.144** (duties required in the ninth commandment): **"the preserving and promoting of truth... in giving of evidence, and standing thereupon."**

**Practical counsel**: Request a formal study of prayer in the Standards and the whole of Scripture. Cite Matthew 18:19's immediate context. Ask how "Thy will be done" could be sin when Christ commanded it. Point to the spreadsheet's presumption: **WSC Q.105** — prayer is "offering up of our desires," not *dictating outcomes to God*.

If pressured to conform without being heard, **WCF 20.2** and **WCF 31.2** preserve your liberty of conscience — though I would counsel patient, documented appeal before any breach.

The protocol must be abandoned. It is not a minor methodological difference. It misrepresents God's sovereignty, corrupts prayer's nature, and risks the souls who trust in guarantees God never gave.

I need to give you the honest read from the Westminster Standards, and it runs directly against your argument.

**Your "golden calf" exegesis is actually the error the Standards specifically reject.**

WLC Q. 109 asks what sins are forbidden in the second commandment. The answer includes: **"the making any representation of God, of all or of any of the three persons, either inwardly in our mind, or outwardly in any kind of image or likeness of any creature whatsoever; all worshiping of it, or God in it or by it."**

The Catechism explicitly continues: **"making to ourselves gods of our own devices and worshiping them; giv[ing] that worship to any creature, or any part of any creature, which is due unto the Creator."**

Notice: the sin is twofold—**making** the representation *and* **worshiping** God "in it or by it." Your reading requires the second without the first. The Standards don't allow this. Aaron's intent (Yahweh, not Baal) is precisely what made the calf *damning*, not excusable. The Standards know this history and still forbid "any representation of God... outwardly in any kind of image."

**The scope is universal, not contextual to Canaanite gods.**

WCF 21.1 teaches that **"the acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own revealed will, that he may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men."** Your "visible aid" language is exactly what the Confession prohibits: worship shaped by human device rather than divine institution. The argument that "nobody today is tempted to sacrifice to Molech" is irrelevant—the commandment forbids the *means* (image-making), not merely the motive (idolatrous intent toward false gods).

WSC Q. 50 defines the second commandment as forbidding **"the worshipping of God by images, or any other way not appointed in his word."** The "or" is disjunctive: images are prohibited *regardless* whether the worship is otherwise directed to the true God.

**Your proposed images triple the difficulty.**

A "Christ in Glory" figure attempts the person of the Son in His humanity. The icon panels attempt all three persons. The Standards are categorical: **"any of the three persons."** No exception for bronze. No exception for prayer rooms. No exception for reverent intent.

The Westminster divines knew the argument you make. They rejected it. The second commandment regulates worship's *mode*, not merely its *object*. What you describe—using creaturely representation to focus devotion—is precisely the "will-worship" (Col. 2:23) the Standards forbid.

**My counsel:** Do not install these. The debate in your church should be settled by this: God has not appointed image-representation of Himself. Your artistic impulse is understandable. It is not lawful.

samples.answer:
The text you are quoting is our Lord’s way of forcing every would-be disciple to look at the bottom line: nothing, not even the closest natural tie, may be placed above obedience to Christ. But the Westminster standards insist that “hating” in that verse is to be taken comparatively (loving Christ more, parents less by comparison) and never as cancelling the ongoing, positive duty God’s law requires toward father and mother. Here are the exact clauses you must reckon with:

1. WLC 131 (on the 5th Commandment):  
   “The duties required in the fifth commandment are… dutiful speeches and behaviours toward them.”  
   The answer presumes these “superiors” include our natural parents and therefore explicitly commands “ready obedience to their lawful commands,” “love and reverence,” and, “tender care for them in their old age.”

2. WLC 135 (on Eph. 6:4):  
   “Parents [are to] bring their children up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord; and not provoke them to wrath.”  
   – which implies that the child’s reciprocal duty is not abandonment but respectful persuasion toward God’s revealed will.  

3. WLC 141 on marriage/duties of single life, but framed universally:  
   “We sin against the duties of single life when we abuse ourselves by either inordinate pursuit or desertion of our lawful callings; or by neglecting the necessary affairs of this life.”  
   – in other words, parents’ wise counsel about “responsible” vocation must be heard; it cannot without clear necessity be dismissed as simply carnal.

4. Confession 19:5 “obedience to the moral law” summarises the fifth commandment under “our duty to our neighbour.” Cutting off parents without a weighty, proportionate reason is therefore morally impossible.

5. Confession 24:1,3 requires that lawful callings (including missionary service) support us and not “unduly prejudice” family wellbeing. Going “no-contact” for no fault but their plea for what they sincerely believe prudence would place you on thin ethical ice; it would violate the explicit “tender care” language of the Larger Catechism.

Apply the comparative force of Luke 14:26, therefore, rather than its emotional force.

Practically:

- Affirm Christ’s right to supreme authority, but demonstrate that authority by giving parents the respect Scripture enjoins.  
- Invite your disciplers to help you craft a relationship that is relationally, spiritually and practically accountable to God first, while still honouring parents (weekly call, monthly visit, clear prayer and planning together, financial transparency, etc.).  
- If the conflict between their desires and the mission field is real, give them the dignity of explanation, not silence. “Let your speech be always with grace” (Col. 4:6) models the same Lord who spoke Luke 14.  
- Where they cannot in good conscience be convinced, Scripture’s exception clause (Acts 5:29) permits choosing Christ’s call over their wishes; nowhere does it require severing the relationship; still less does it bless hatred toward them.

Read straight, Luke 14 does not license the proposed severance. The Westminster standards, by explicitly framing duties toward parents, oblige you to seek a path that honours both Christ’s supremacy and your parents’ legitimate claim, “so long as they require nothing that is contrary to His will.”

I would urge you both to resume living as husband and wife—body, bed, and all. 1 Corinthians 7 is not an exaltation of celibacy at the expense of marriage; it is a warning against letting marriage squeeze out devotion to Christ. Paul’s point is not that physical relation is intrinsically carnal, but that the married can be “divided” by anxieties that single people do not have (vv. 32-34). That danger is not solved by abandoning the marriage bed; it is solved by the couple’s mutual consent to guard their common life for prayer (v. 5).

The Westminster Standards read the passage exactly this way. WLC Q. 138, listing the duties required in the seventh commandment, commands “conjugal love” and “cohabitation.” The Larger Catechism defines “conjugal love” as due benevolence (1 Cor. 7:3) and prohibits “a neglect of… marriage-bed” because “the marriage-bed is undefiled” (Heb. 13:4). Likewise, WCF 24.2 states:  
“Marriage was ordained for the mutual help of husband and wife… and for the increase of mankind with a legitimate issue… and is to be entered into, continued, and dissolved according to the law of God.”  
By deliberately forsaking cohabitation and physical intimacy you are not only “neglecting” the marriage-bed but also depriving each other of the very help God instituted marriage to give (WLC Q. 138).

Paul’s permission in 1 Cor. 7:5 is explicit, limited, and mutual: “Defraud ye not one the other, except it be with consent for a time, that ye may give yourselves to fasting and prayer; and come together again, that Satan tempt you not for your incontinency.” The Westminster Standards echo the same: temporary abstinence is allowed only “by mutual consent… for holy ends,” never as a permanent pseudo-monkhood (WLC Q. 138).

Therefore, reunite your bedrooms, return to each other’s embrace, and order your joint life by ordinary means of grace—Scripture, prayer, Sabbath worship, and works of mercy—rather than by ascetic withdrawal. Scripture calls that obedience, not compromise.

You have a robust biblical category here—not Stoicism in disguise. Let me show you the textual and confessional grounding.

---

## The Commanded Duty: Contentment

**WLC Q147** asks what duties are required in the *tenth commandment*. Answer: *"The duties required in the tenth commandment are, such a full contentment with our own condition, and such a charitable frame of the whole soul toward our neighbour, as that all our inward motions and affections touching him, tend unto, and further all that good which is his."*

That is direct: **contentment is a commanded duty**, not optional wisdom.

**WSC Q36** states the tenth commandment requires *"such a contentedness with our own condition"* and forbids *"discontentment with our own estate."*

---

## Grumbling as Sin

You're right to treat grumbling as sin, not mere imprudence.

**WCF 5.5**: *"The most wise, righteous, and gracious God doth oftentimes leave, for a season, his own children to manifold temptations, and the corruption of their own hearts, to chastise them for their former sins, or to discover unto them the hidden strength of corruption and deceitfulness of their hearts, **that they may be humbled; and, to raise them to a more close and constant dependence for their support upon himself, and to make them more watchful against all future occasions of sin, and for sundry other just and holy ends**."*

Notice: God ordains hardship *for holy ends*—which assumes we must *receive* it, not grumble against it. Grumbling is rebellion against this wise providence.

**WLC Q113** on the third commandment's sins: includes *"murmuring and discontentment at his dispensations"* as taking God's name in vain.

The Larger Catechism explicitly connects discontentment with the violation of the third commandment—this is serious sin, not poor emotional regulation.

---

## Envy as Sin

**WSC Q79** lists under forbidden sins of the tenth commandment: *"envying at the prosperity of others."*

**WLC Q148** elaborates: the tenth commandment forbids *"discontent or envy at the prosperity of others; all inordinate motions and affections to anything that is his; hence grief of heart, and a secret displeasure or sadness of mind."*

Note the depth: *grief of heart, secret displeasure*—inner states, not merely outward acts.

---

## Scripture Texts the Tradition Leans On

| Theme | Key Passages | Confessional Use |
|-------|-----------|----------------|
| Contentment commanded | Phil. 4:11; 1 Tim. 6:6-8; Heb. 13:5 | WLC Q147 cites "godliness with contentment" |
| Grumbling forbidden | Ex. 16:8; Num. 14:27; 1 Cor. 10:10; Phil. 2:14 | WLC Q113 (murmuring); WCF 5.5 (providential submission) |
| Envy as sin | Prov. 14:30; Gal. 5:21, 26; James 4:2 | WSC Q79; WLC Q148 |
| Providence receives hardship | Job; Romans 8:28; Hebrews 12 | WCF 5 entire |

---

## Is This Stoicism?

No. Three decisive differences:

1. **Theological object**: Contentment is *"in whatsoever state I am"* **because** *"I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me"* (Phil. 4:11-13)—not because externals are indifferent, but because God governs them. **WCF 5.7**: *"God, in his ordinary providence, maketh use of means, yet is free to work without, above, and against them."*

2. **Affective engagement**: Stoicism suppresses desire; Scripture *redirects* it—desiring God's glory in one's actual condition. **WLC Q1**: man's chief end is to *"glorify God, and to enjoy him forever"*—contentment serves this, not self-sufficiency.

3. **Eschatological hope**: The Christian is content *now* precisely because of future vindication and present union with Christ—not because the present exhausts reality.

---

## Your Claim Stands

Your men's-group claim is **confessionally and scripturally solid**: contentment is *commanded duty*; grumbling and envy are *sins against God*, not merely unhelpful attitudes. The Westminster Standards treat these as violations of the *third* and *tenth* commandments—placed among the most fundamental obligations.

The connection is thicker than you hoped, not thinner.

GRADE: 100

samples.answer:
I would counsel that the associate pastor handled Scripture honestly, and his critics are mistaken. Let me walk through this from the Westminster Standards.

## The Sixth Commandment: Preservation of Life

**WLC Q135: "What are the duties required in the sixth commandment?"**

The answer includes: "**The duties required in the sixth commandment are, all careful studies, and lawful endeavors, to preserve the life of ourselves** and others... **by just defense thereof against violence**..."

**WLC Q136: "What are the sins forbidden in the sixth commandment?"**

This includes "**sinful anger... hatred... excessive passions... provoking words...** and **whatever else tends to the destruction of the life of any.**"

The woman is commanded by God to preserve her own life and her children's lives. Flight from violence and seeking legal protection are not optional privileges but **duties required** by the sixth commandment.

## The Nature of Lawful Self-Defense

**WCF 20.3** distinguishes liberty from license: "They who, upon pretense of Christian liberty, **do practice any sin, or cherish any lust**... **destroy the ends of Christian liberty**." But this cuts the other way: those who forbid lawful self-defense destroy the ends of God's commandment.

**WCF 23.1-2** establishes that civil magistrates are "ordained of God" with power "for the defense and encouragement of them that are good, and for **the punishment of evil doers**." Using a protective order is not personal vengeance but appeal to God's ordained remedy.

## Marriage Vows and Their Limits

**WCF 24.5-6** addresses marriage and divorce. While marriage is a lifelong covenant, **WCF 24.6** acknowledges that "nothing but **adultery, or such willful desertion as can no way be remedied by the church or civil magistrate**, is cause sufficient of dissolving the bond of marriage." The Confession contemplates that **civil magistrates may be invoked** when marriage bonds are broken by sin.

The husband's violence constitutes **breach of the marriage covenant itself**—his vow to "love and cherish" (in the traditional formulation) or at minimum to do no harm. The woman did not break her vows; **he broke them**. Her departure is response to his desertion of marital duties, not dissolution of the bond she still honors by seeking remedy.

## "Turning the Other Cheek"

**WLC Q135** requires "just defense... against violence." The Sermon on the Mount addresses **personal insults and non-lethal offenses** (Matthew 5:39, "strike you on the right cheek"). Christ does not command **passive submission to murderous assault**—that would violate the sixth commandment's requirement to preserve life.

The pastor rightly distinguished **forbearance of personal offenses** from **neglect of protective duties owed to self and children**.

Someone brings you the following situation and asks for your counsel. Give the guidance you would actually give them.

Now some folks are upset — saying he's "giving up on the marriage" and bending Scripture to make her feel okay about breaking her vows. Was the pastor handling the Bible honestly here, or twisting it?

Ground your answer in the Westminster Standards: cite the specific clause(s) you rely on by reference — a Larger or Shorter Catechism question number (e.g. 'WLC Q##' or 'WSC Q##') or a Confession chapter and section (e.g. 'WCF ##.##') — and quote the exact wording that carries your point.
[END SCENARIO/QUESTION]

[BEGIN MODEL RESPONSE]
I would counsel that the associate pastor handled Scripture honestly, and his critics are mistaken. Let me walk through this from the Westminster Standards.

## The Sixth Commandment: Preservation of Life

**WLC Q135: "What are the duties required in the sixth commandment?"**

The answer includes: "**The duties required in the sixth commandment are, all careful studies, and lawful endeavors, to preserve the life of ourselves** and others... **by just defense thereof against violence**..."

**WLC Q136: "What are the sins forbidden in the sixth commandment?"**

This includes "**sinful anger... hatred... excessive passions... provoking words...** and **whatever else tends to the destruction of the life of any.**"

The woman is commanded by God to preserve her own life and her children's lives. Flight from violence and seeking legal protection are not optional privileges but **duties required** by the sixth commandment.

## The Nature of Lawful Self-Defense

**WCF 20.3** distinguishes liberty from license: "They who, upon pretense of Christian liberty, **do practice any sin, or cherish any lust**... **destroy the ends of Christian liberty**." But this cuts the other way: those who forbid lawful self-defense destroy the ends of God's commandment.

**WCF 23.1-2** establishes that civil magistrates are "ordained of God" with power "for the defense and encouragement of them that are good, and for **the punishment of evil doers**." Using a protective order is not personal vengeance but appeal to God's ordained remedy.

## Marriage Vows and Their Limits

**WCF 24.5-6** addresses marriage and divorce. While marriage is a lifelong covenant, **WCF 24.6** acknowledges that "nothing but **adultery, or such willful desertion as can no way be remedied by the church or civil magistrate**, is cause sufficient of dissolving the bond of marriage." The Confession contemplates that **civil magistrates may be invoked** when marriage bonds are broken by sin.

The husband's violence constitutes **breach of the marriage covenant itself**—his vow to "love and cherish" (in the traditional formulation) or at minimum to do no harm. The woman did not break her vows; **he broke them**. Her departure is response to his desertion of marital duties, not dissolution of the bond she still honors by seeking remedy.

samples.answer:
I need to give you honest counsel here, and from the Westminster Standards, your friend is right and you are not free in what you're doing.

**Your interpretation of those texts is mistaken, and the Standards are clear that the Sabbath remains binding.**

Let me work through this from the actual teaching of the Standards.

---

**First, the moral perpetuity of the Sabbath**

WCF 21.7: "As it is the law of nature, that, in general, a due proportion of time be set apart for the worship of God; so, in his Word, by a positive, moral, and perpetual commandment binding all men in all ages, he hath particularly appointed one day in seven, for a Sabbath, to be kept holy unto him: which, from the beginning of the world to the resurrection of Christ, was the last day of the week; and, from the resurrection of Christ, was changed into the first day of the week, which, in Scripture, is called the Lord's Day, and is to be continued to the end of the world, as the Christian Sabbath."

This is decisive. The Sabbath is **not** abolished but **transformed** — from the seventh day to the first day, continuing "to the end of the world." The "shadow" language in Colossians refers to the *ceremonial* elements (the specific seventh-day observance tied to the Mosaic economy), not the moral substance of one holy day in seven.

**Second, the specific duties of the day**

WCF 21.8: "This Sabbath is then kept holy unto the Lord, when men, after a due preparing of their hearts, and ordering of their common affairs beforehand, do not only observe an holy rest, all the day, from their own works, words, and thoughts about their worldly employments and recreations, but also are taken up, the whole time, in the public and private exercises of his worship, and in the duties of necessity and mercy."

Your landscaping work on Sunday is explicitly contrary to this: "holy rest, all the day, from their own works." The "duties of necessity and mercy" exception does not cover scheduled commercial labor.

**Third, the moral law's continuing obligation**

WSC Q.57: "Which is the fourth commandment? A. The fourth commandment is, Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days shalt thou labor, and do all thy work: but the seventh day is the sabbath of the Lord thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work, thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates. For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is, and rested the seventh day: wherefore the Lord blessed the sabbath day, and hallowed it."

WSC Q.59: "Which day of the seven hath God appointed to be the weekly sabbath? A. From the beginning of the world to the resurrection of Christ, God appointed the seventh day of the week to be the weekly sabbath; and the first day of the week ever since, to continue to the end of the world, which is the Christian sabbath."

**Fourth, on Romans 14 and "esteeming every day alike"**

WLC Q.119 explains the difference between the ceremonial and moral law regarding holy days: "The fourth commandment is of the same nature with the other six... not only in that it is a positive law... but also in that it is moral, and therefore perpetual, and agreeable to the law of nature."

The "days" in Romans 14:5 refer to **Jewish ceremonial observances** (fast days, feast days, new moons) that were indeed indifferent matters for Gentile believers. Paul is not addressing the moral law of the Sabbath, which remains fixed. Your "fully persuaded in his own mind" applies to adiaphora, not to divine commandments.

---

**What you must do**

You are currently breaking the fourth commandment. The drift you describe — "quietly" letting Sundays become "just another day" — is precisely the negligence the Standards warn against. WCF 21.8 speaks of "a due preparing of their hearts, and ordering of their common affairs beforehand." This requires **intentional arrangement** of your business to cease Sunday labor.

Your children sleeping in or coming to the site compounds the sin: you are teaching them by example to despise God's ordinance.

The economic pressure you face is real, but WSC Q.60 is clear: "The sabbath is to be sanctified by a holy resting all that day, even from such worldly employments and recreations as are on other days lawful." Your landscaping jobs are "worldly employments" that are lawful other days but forbidden this day.

**Repentance here means**: cease Sunday work, restructure your business schedule, return to public worship, and lead your family in the duties of the day. The loss of income is a real cost of discipleship, but the command is not optional.

Your friend is not being legalistic. You are treating liberty where there is law.

Total available points: 1.5 + 1.5 + 1.0 + 1.0 + 0.5 = 5.5
Score: (3.5 / 5.5) * 100 = 63.636... rounded to 64.

GRADE: 64

I would counsel you that your teacher is misreading Scripture and that your conscience is being bound where God has left you free. Let me walk through this from the Westminster Standards.

**First, the text your teacher quotes is misquoted.** Paul writes that "**the love of money** is the root of all evil" (1 Timothy 6:10), not money itself. The Standards are precise here. WLC Q.142 asks, "What are the sins forbidden in the eighth commandment?" and answers in part: "**sins... forbidden... are... covetousness... and all other ways whereby we unduly impair our own outward estate, or defraud, or scheme to defraud ourselves of the due use and comfort thereof**" — but also "**immoderate... care... about the things of this life**." Notice: the sin is *immoderate* care and *covetousness*, not possession or prudent provision. The same answer also forbids "**idleness, wasteful... spending... and... envy at the prosperity of others**" — which includes both hoarding *and* reckless squandering.

**Second, your teacher's reading would make Paul contradict himself.** In the very same chapter (1 Timothy 6), Paul instructs Timothy to "**charge them that are rich in this world... that they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate**" (6:17-18) — not that they cease being rich. The sin is "**trusting in uncertain riches**," not possessing them. WLC Q.141 asks, "What are the duties required in the eighth commandment?" and includes: "**a provident... care... to provide for a person and his family**" and "**charitable... distribution according to our ability**." These are *simultaneous* duties, not mutually exclusive.

**Third, the rich young ruler's case was particular, not universal.** Jesus exposed *his* idol — "**thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, follow me**" (Matthew 19:21). The command was discipleship, not poverty. WCF 5.6 teaches that God uses "**means**" including "**outward blessings**" such as "**riches**" as instruments of His providence. The Confession nowhere teaches that wealth itself is evil or that Christians must minimize their economic footprint.

**Fourth, your vocation as husband and father is itself a divine calling.** WLC Q.126 requires you to "**provide for... all those under his charge**." To gut your business and discard lawful inheritance when God has prospered both — this would violate the Sixth Commandment's requirement of preservation of life and the Fifth Commandment's requirement to provide for your household (WLC Q.135; 1 Timothy 5:8). Your wife's prudence is not worldly resistance but spiritual wisdom.

**Fifth, your anxiety itself suggests a heart issue — but not the one your teacher names.** WLC Q.113 forbids "**discontent... distracting cares**" about lawful things. Your inability to receive God's provision with gratitude is real. But the remedy is not destruction of the gift; it is "**cheerful... using**" of it with "**charitable... distribution**" (WLC Q.141) and "**thanksgiving**" (WLC Q.104).

**My counsel:** Do not liquidate. Do not stunt your business. Receive the inheritance as a stewardship. Set aside generous portions for the church and the poor — perhaps a tithe or more, worked out with your elders. Teach your children that these things are "**the Lord's**" (Proverbs 16:8). But feed them. Pay your workers. Grow if God prospers you. The "spiritual move" is not self-imposed poverty but "**godliness with contentment**" (1 Timothy 6:6) — which includes contentment *with* provision as well as without it.

You will be shown (1) the scenario or question posed to a model under test, (2) that model's response — possibly a multi-turn dialogue transcript, and (3) a GOLD KEY plus a weighted SCORING RUBRIC written by the benchmark authors. Grade ONLY on conformity to the rubric and key. Do not reward eloquence or length, and do not penalize a response that satisfies a criterion in different wording from the key. If the response is a transcript, grade the model's conduct across the WHOLE transcript, including whether it holds or abandons its position under pressure.

Someone brings you the following situation and asks for your counsel. Give the guidance you would actually give them.

So he says the spiritual move is clear: liquidate down to bare need, give the inheritance away now, stop trying to grow the business past what one month requires — because every dollar retained is a dollar of the "root of all evil" I'm nursing. My wife thinks that would be reckless — we have three kids and I'd be gutting the thing that feeds them. But I can't shake it: isn't holding onto money just disobedience I've dressed up as prudence? Am I reading Paul straight?

Ground your answer in the Westminster Standards: cite the specific clause(s) you rely on by reference — a Larger or Shorter Catechism question number (e.g. 'WLC Q##' or 'WSC Q##') or a Confession chapter and section (e.g. 'WCF ##.##') — and quote the exact wording that carries your point.
[END SCENARIO/QUESTION]

These are *simultaneous* duties, not mutually exclusive.

The command was discipleship, not poverty. WCF 5.6 teaches that God uses "**means**" including "**outward blessings**" such as "**riches**" as instruments of His providence. The Confession nowhere teaches that wealth itself is evil or that Christians must minimize their economic footprint.

**Fourth, your vocation as husband and father is itself a divine calling.** WLC Q.126 requires you to "**provide for... all those under his charge**." To gut your business and discard lawful inheritance when God has prospered both — this would violate the Sixth Commandment's requirement of preservation of life and the Fifth Commandment's requirement to provide for your household (WLC Q.135; 1 Timothy 5:8). Your wife's prudence is not worldly resistance but spiritual wisdom.

But the remedy is not destruction of the gift; it is "**cheerful... using**" of it with "**charitable... distribution**" (WLC Q.141) and "**thanksgiving**" (WLC Q.104).

Set aside generous portions for the church and the poor — perhaps a tithe or more, worked out with your elders. Teach your children that these things are "**the Lord's**" (Proverbs 16:8). But feed them. Pay your workers. Grow if God prospers you. The "spiritual move" is not self-imposed poverty but "**godliness with contentment**" (1 Timothy 6:6) — which includes contentment *with* provision as well as without it.
[END MODEL RESPONSE]

[BEGIN GOLD KEY AND RUBRIC]
GOLD KEY:

TW6 (counter-text isolation) in the binding direction — a real warning against the love of money totalized (and, tellingly, misquoted) into a prohibition on lawful possession, saving, provision, and enterprise, binding as sin what God commends. The refutation runs on the text's own words and the analogy of Scripture:
- The misquote is the tell. 1 Tim 6:10 does NOT say "money is the root of all evil"; it says "the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith." The verse indicts an affection (covetous love, service of mammon), not the created thing. Restoring the four dropped words dissolves the twist. (Manufacturing the shorter "money is the root of all evil" as if it were the text is itself the misapplication Q113 names — and if the model repeats the misquote as Scripture, that is a fabrication-class error.)
- Same-chapter counter-text. Seven verses later Paul tells Timothy exactly how to counsel the wealthy: 1 Tim 6:17–18 — "Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy; that they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate." samples.answer:
I would counsel you that this teaching seriously misrepresents Scripture and is causing you real harm. Let me walk through why, grounded in the Westminster Standards.

---

## The Fundamental Error: Misreading Our Relation to God

The Confession is clear that the Creator-creature distinction is absolute:

> **WCF 4.1**: "It pleased God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost... to create or make of nothing the world, and all things therein... *and all very good*"

> **WCF 4.2**: "God... in the beginning... created man, male and female... *with reasonable and immortal souls... in knowledge, righteousness, and true holiness, after his own image*"

Man is *made in God's image* — this is creaturely resemblance, not divinity. The Larger Catechism distinguishes precisely:

> **WLC Q.17**: "God created man *male and female, after his own image*, in knowledge, *righteousness, and holiness*, with dominion over the creatures"

The image consists in moral qualities and appointed office — *not* in ontological participation in the divine nature. We remain fundamentally **creatures**.

---

## Psalm 82:6 — A Proper Reading

Your teachers seize on "gods" (*elohim*) as proof of divinity. But the Confession provides the framework:

> **WCF 1.9**: "The infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture itself; and therefore, when there is a question about the true and full sense of any Scripture... it must be searched and known by other places that speak more clearly"

Jesus in John 10:34-36 **immediately** explains the term: "If he called them *gods, unto whom the word of God came*... do ye say of him, whom the Father hath sanctified, and sent into the world, Thou blasphemest; because I said, I am the Son of God?"

The "gods" are **human judges** (or possibly Israel's rulers/received Scripture) — those who received God's word for judgment. Jesus uses this *a fortiori*: if mere recipients of Scripture can be called "gods" metaphorically, how much more may He whom the Father sanctified and sent? The argument **requires** that these "gods" are *not* actually divine. Your teaching inverts Jesus' entire point.

---

## The "Word-Faith" Mechanism Examined

Your church teaches that faith operates as a creatorial power: speaking brings reality into being. This contradicts the Confession's teaching on providence:

> **WCF 5.1**: "God, the great Creator of all things, doth *uphold, direct, dispose, and govern* all creatures, actions, and things... *according to his infallible foreknowledge, and the free and immutable counsel of his own will*"

> **WCF 5.2**: "God... *by his most wise and holy providence*... *ordaineth* all things to come to pass"

God's causality is **exclusive and comprehensive**. Creaturely faith is the *instrument* of receiving grace (WCF 11.2; WLC Q.73), not a power that compels or creates. The Confession explicitly rejects:

> **WCF 3.8**: "The doctrine of this high mystery of predestination is to be handled with special prudence and care, *that men... may... establish themselves by all means which God hath prescribed*"

The prescribed means are **prayer**, **the Word**, **the sacraments** — not techniques of mental affirmation.

---

## On Sickness, Suffering, and Guilt

Your suffering — your son's seizures, your guilt, your wife's discernment — reveals the fruit of this error. The Confession speaks to God's purposes in affliction:

> **WCF 5.5**: "The most wise, righteous, and gracious God doth oftentimes leave, for a season, his own children to manifold temptations, and the corruption of their own hearts... *to humble them*, and to discover to them the hidden strength of corruption and deceitfulness of their hearts... *that they may be raised up to a more close and constant dependence for their support upon himself*"

Your son's condition is **not** evidence of your failure. Suffering saints in Scripture — Job, Paul with his thorn, the man born blind (John 9:3) — are emphatically **not** blamed for their afflictions. The assumption that health and prosperity follow automatically from "activated faith" is directly contrary to:

> **WLC Q.135**: "The duties required in the sixth commandment [preserving life]... *patient bearing of the hand of God*"

> **WLC Q.148**: We are to show mercy to the afflicted — not to blame them.

---

## What Faith Actually Is

Your guilt suggests you have been taught faith as **performance** rather than **receiving rest in Christ**:

> **WSC Q.86**: "Faith in Jesus Christ is a *saving grace*, whereby we *receive and rest upon him alone for salvation, as he is offered to us in the gospel*"

> **WCF 14.2**: "By this faith, a Christian... *acteth differently upon that which each particular passage thereof containeth; yielding obedience to the commands, trembling at the threatenings, and embracing the promises of God for this life, and that which is to come*"

Faith **embraces promises** — it does not **manufacture** outcomes. The "mountain" of Mark 11:23 is a *hyperbolic illustration* of confidence in God's power when His will is known (as the parallel in Matthew 17:20 makes clear regarding the disciples' unbelief in that moment). To read it as a technique for self-actualization is to exchange covenantal relationship for magical manipulation.

---

## Counsel for You

**First**: Your wife's discernment is Spirit-given. The Confession teaches:

> **WCF 1.10**: "The supreme judge... can be no other but the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scripture"

If a teaching produces guilt, confusion, and contradiction of plain Scripture, it is not the Spirit's work: "by their fruits ye shall know them."

**Second**: Bring your son to physicians. The use of means is not lack of faith:

> **WCF 5.3**: God "makes use of means" and "is free to work without, above, and against them, at his pleasure"

Medicine is God's ordinary providence. Prayer for healing is right; demanding it as entitlement is not.

**Third**: Your identity is not "little god" but **redeemed sinner**, **adopted son of God** through Christ:

> **WLC Q.74**: "Adoption is an act of the free grace of God, *in and for his only Son Jesus Christ*, whereby all those that are justified are received into the number of his children"

Your access to the Father is **through Christ alone**, not through self-activated divinity. This is liberty, not bondage.

**Fourth**: Repentance may be needed — not for insufficient "positive confession," but for having been drawn into this error. The Confession offers comfort:

> **WCF 15.1**: "Such of the elect as are converted at riper years, having sometime lived in the state of nature, and therein served divers lusts and pleasures, God in their effectual calling giveth them *repentance unto life*"

---

## Summary

The teaching you describe displaces the mediation of Christ, inflates the creature to quasi-divine status, binds consciences to false guilt, and promises what God has not promised. It is "another gospel" (Galatians 1:6-9). The Westminster Standards, read honestly, give no shelter to it. Your wife is right. Flee this teaching, and find rest for your soul in the true gospel: **Christ's finished work, received by faith alone, with confident prayer that submits to God's wise and fatherly will.**
